doc.title: Bob Hardaway interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999

title: Union pit scales, traveling shows and recorded music
summary: Theater pit contracts vary by theater owner, and traveling shows used to have to hire local players. The union lost a picket over a taped Rockettes show, and synthesizers replace strings.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Do you know if the union has a minimum requirement for people in the pits these days?

Yes they do. And they vary. There’s different contracts. There’s the Nederlander Corporation has some theaters and then there’s other groups that have other theaters, and each one of those is a separate negotiation also. And they have to negotiate for the pit. And then another problem they have is when a traveling show comes in it used to be that they’d have to pay a certain number of local musicians, even though they didn’t play. I mean that’s because they were displacing jobs by bringing a traveling orchestra in. And I’m not sure, I think that’s different now, that’s changed. I’ve been out of that field for a long time. But when they bring the whole thing, or they bring a track, the whole thing recorded. Now we were picketing just a couple of months ago when the Rockettes show was here. And it appeared over at the Universal Ampitheater. And they had a completely recorded—
Taped music for these people dancing. And part of the excitement is the live music you know I would think. But we lost.
Yeah. We couldn’t get anything done about it.

Well I noticed from where we live that the shows will come in and the number of real live people in the pits for those traveling shows has sunk to almost nothing. The electronics have replaced people like crazy.

Sure. Well they usually do it without strings at all, and just use the synthesizers for the string sounds, which are probably closer to sounding reasonable than the woodwinds. They don’t seem to be able to get the woodwinds, there’s something about the overtones or something that is hard for them to get, thankfully.
It’s too bad people in the audience don’t stand up and say that’s not real.

Well they don’t really know. So many motion pictures are being made right now, this is a very busy field, that’s one of the busiest things in this town, they’re making a lot of motion pictures. Lots of them. And almost all of them, every one I see, a lot of it is electric music. And then conversely, they’ll have hundred-piece orchestras on some of them. So I don’t know.
